title: "O fim dos tratamentos não significa o fim do sofrimento"
content:
Este artigo faz parte da série “O que eu aprendi com a dor dos outros”, um conjunto de reportagens escritas por uma jornalista a partir de entrevistas com profissionais de saúde que acompanham doentes com dor crónica.
Quando digo a alguém que está em remissão, isso é uma excelente notícia, mas não significa necessariamente “agora está tudo bem”. É por isso que defendo que o objetivo do tratamento passa, não apenas pelo prolongamento da sobrevivência, mas também pelo controlo da doença, pela redução dos sintomas e pela preservação da qualidade de vida do doente.
Tenho 49 anos e quando terminei o curso de Medicina, comecei por escolher a infeciologia como especialidade, mas depois decidi mudar para a especialidade de oncologia médica. Hoje trabalho sobretudo com sarcomas, um tipo de tumor que pode surgir nos ossos ou nos tecidos moles, com tumores urológicos (como os da próstata, bexiga, rim e testículo) e com tumores neuroendócrinos.
Nestas mais de duas décadas de profissão, muita coisa mudou. Temos mais alternativas terapêuticas e investigação. Isto tem aumentado não apenas os anos que os doentes vivem, mas também o número de sobreviventes de cancro.
Cada vez mais pessoas vivem muitos anos depois de um diagnóstico de cancro — umas sem doença, mas com sequelas, outras com uma doença metastática controlada — e isso criou uma nova necessidade: acompanhar os sobreviventes.
Quem teve um cancro pode ficar com sequelas dos tratamentos, ter de lidar com uma ansiedade incapacitante, manter comportamentos de risco que convém mudar ou sentir dificuldades em regressar à vida profissional, familiar e social. Foi por isso que na CUF Descobertas e na CUF Tejo foi criada a Unidade do Sobrevivente de Cancro, onde uma equipa multidisciplinar, com profissionais de várias áreas, faz consultas que já não estão focadas no tratamento, mas em ajudar a pessoa com estes problemas físicos, psicológicos e/ou sociais.
“‘Já não tem cancro, vá à sua vida.’ Não podemos dizer isso”
O fim dos tratamentos e a remissão do cancro fecham um capítulo, mas raramente são o fim da história. Ter um cancro e tratar a doença tem um impacto significativo na vida da pessoa. Desde logo porque há pessoas que ficam com sequelas dos tratamentos como amputações, neuropatia, dor crónica e distúrbios hormonais.
Há ainda consequências que são menos óbvias, mas igualmente importantes como problemas de infertilidade, alterações da vida sexual e da relação com o próprio corpo também. Além disso, é possível que ocorram problemas psicológicos e sociais: muitos doentes experienciam problemas de ansiedade, sintomas de depressão e dificuldade em regressar ao trabalho.
O fim dos tratamentos não significa necessariamente o fim do sofrimento. Durante o tratamento, a pessoa está muito focada em sobreviver, em fazer tudo o que é preciso: os exames, a cirurgia, a quimioterapia, mais exames. Depois chega o dia em que terminam os tratamentos e fica em vigilância ou tem alta da consulta de oncologia e a pessoa pensa: “Mas eu não estou igual.” Acaba por se sentir desamparada e é aí que uma unidade de sobreviventes pode fazer a diferença.
Temos oncologistas, enfermeiros, nutricionistas, profissionais ligados ao exercício físico, fisioterapeutas, psicólogos, psiquiatras, sexólogos, anestesistas, endocrinologistas e outros profissionais, consoante as necessidades de cada pessoa. A vantagem de termos todos estes profissionais envolvidos numa unidade destas é a experiência e o conhecimento que se adquire e partilha sobre as necessidades particulares de quem passou por um cancro.
Por exemplo, há quem precise de fisioterapia para recuperar uma limitação ou para se adaptar a uma prótese. Há quem precise de ajuda para controlar uma dor crónica. Há pessoas que ficam com dor fantasma depois de uma amputação — a parte do corpo já não está lá, mas a dor continua. Há quem precise de acompanhamento psicológico. Muitas pessoas precisam de ajuda para deixar de fumar, reduzir o consumo de álcool ou mudar a alimentação.
As pessoas já não estão necessariamente doentes, mas continuam a precisar de cuidados de saúde. Não podemos dizer: “Já não tem cancro, vá à sua vida.”
“Sabemos muito pouco. E não há nada de errado em admiti-lo”
A dor em oncologia pode vir do próprio tumor ou surgir depois, no decurso dos tratamentos e cirurgias. Não é igual para todos. Duas pessoas com o mesmo tumor, na mesma localização, que fizeram o mesmo tratamento podem ter experiências completamente diferentes. Há pessoas que, perante uma doença que eu imagino ser muito dolorosa, dizem que não têm dor; outras, com situações aparentemente menos graves, têm dores muito intensas. Por isso, a dor que eu trato é a dor que o doente me relata.
Há dores que exigem medicamentos específicos, outras em que precisamos de recorrer a bloqueios nervosos e há situações em que o exercício, a medicina física e de reabilitação ou o apoio de outras áreas podem ser fundamentais.
Lembro-me de um doente jovem, com um sarcoma muito extenso, que teve de ser amputado. Mesmo depois da amputação, continuava a sentir dor na perna que já não tinha. Era uma dor fantasma, muito intensa, e nós fomos percebendo que não bastava aumentar a medicação. Tivemos o apoio de psicólogos, de um psiquiatra e de um enfermeiro que fazia hipnose. Aos poucos, conseguimos ajudá-lo a reduzir alguns medicamentos e a trabalhar aquela sensação de que o membro continuava ali. Foi um daqueles casos em que percebi, mais uma vez, que não conseguimos tratar a dor de uma só maneira.
Talvez a principal coisa que a Oncologia me tenha ensinado seja precisamente que sabemos muito pouco. E não há nada de errado em admiti-lo. Se tenho dúvidas, pergunto. Se é uma situação rara, vou estudar. Se acho que isso pode fazer a diferença, vou aconselhar-me com colegas.
Precisamos de continuar a ler, a investigar e a perguntar. É preciso ter essa humildade porque, no fim, o que interessa é ajudar o melhor possível a pessoa que está à nossa frente.
“Ser bom médico passa por saber ouvir o doente”
Que tipo de médica sou eu? Uma médica que gosta de ver doentes. É assim que me defino. Faço uma série de outras coisas pois, além do meu trabalho na CUF, dou aulas, faço investigação, e, neste momento, sou diretora do Programa Nacional para as Doenças Oncológicas, da Direção-Geral da Saúde. E tudo isto é muito importante, mas o que me dá mais prazer é ver os meus doentes.
Se nos preocupamos em fazer bem o nosso trabalho, temos de ter tempo para ouvir as pessoas. As preocupações do médico e as do doente nem sempre são as mesmas. Ser bom médico passa por saber ouvir o doente, dar espaço à pessoa para dizer o que a preocupa e, depois, tentar dar resposta a isso.
Lembro-me de um senhor que já estava muito mal e a quem, do ponto de vista de cura da doença, não tínhamos nada para oferecer. A minha preocupação com ele era o controlo dos sintomas, mas a preocupação dele era outra: queria deixar a mulher e os filhos assegurados do ponto de vista financeiro. Disse-me isto, que nunca mais esqueço: “Arranje-me mais algum tempo. Só lhe peço que encontre uma forma de me manter vivo mais um mês, para eu conseguir terminar este processo e deixar o futuro da minha mulher e dos meus filhos assegurado.”
Isto é uma coisa difícil de ouvir, porque a vida e a morte não dependem de mim. Mas era a preocupação dele e lembro-me que, mal o ouvi, pensei: “Como é que eu vou conseguir mais um mês a este senhor?” Felizmente, foi possível. Fiz-lhe umas transfusões e conseguimos ganhar esse tempo.
Eu costumo dizer aos meus alunos e aos médicos mais novos: “Temos de nos preocupar com os doentes.” Ser médico é querer saber. Claro que temos de aprender a fazê-lo sem que isso nos destrua, mas a verdade é que muito do que fazemos nasce dessa preocupação. Se me preocupo, vou ouvir, estudar, investigar, envolver-me em ensaios clínicos, tirar dúvidas com colegas. Vou fazer tudo o que puder para saber dar resposta a esta pergunta: “O que é que eu posso fazer por esta pessoa?”
Porque hoje os doentes estão do outro lado da nossa secretária, mas amanhã podemos ser nós, um amigo ou um familiar. E, nessa altura, também é isso que vamos querer: um médico que se preocupe.
Dor é uma secção do Observador dedicada exclusivamente a temas relacionados com a dor e respetivo acompanhamento clínico e impacto na sociedade. Resulta de uma parceria com a Ferraz Lynce (através da sua unidade, FAI Therapeutics) e tem a colaboração da Associação Portuguesa para o Estudo da Dor e da SIP-Portugal. title: What’s at Risk Under the CRA Proposal and How Communities Can Respond
content:
Congress enacted the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) in 1977 to combat lending discrimination known as redlining. CRA requires federal bank regulators to evaluate whether banks help meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods.
On Aug. 12, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) published a proposed rule that would dramatically weaken banks’ obligations to invest in working-class communities. The Federal Reserve, which administers CRA for the banks it supervises, did not join. The OCC and FDIC say the changes would refocus oversight on local credit needs, ensure community development grants benefit their intended communities, and reduce regulatory burdens, particularly for community banks. In my view, the proposal would instead sharply weaken scrutiny of banks’ lending, services, and community development.
In 2020, when CRA faced a similar threat during President Donald Trump’s first administration, Miriam Axel-Lute noted in Shelterforce that during good times when CRA support is solid, community developers often take CRA’s “pivotal role for granted.” Much of the housing and community development field, she added, rests on a foundation of CRA regulations. That foundation is again at risk.
What the Proposal Would Do
According to preliminary analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), where I serve as president and CEO, the proposal would reduce CRA requirements for hundreds of banks by raising the asset thresholds that determine which examinations and reporting rules they face. Under current rules, banks with less than $412 million generally receive only the small-bank lending test. Banks with at least $412 million but less than $1.649 billion are classified as intermediate small banks and also receive a community development test. Banks with $1.649 billion or more are treated as large and face separate lending, investment, and service tests. The proposal would classify banks with less than $1 billion in assets as small, those with $1 billion to $10 billion as intermediate, and those with more than $10 billion as large.
The classifications may sound very technical, but they determine the CRA tests and reporting requirements each bank faces. Reclassifying banks would reduce scrutiny of community development, branch services, and lending data.
The $1 billion threshold would eliminate community development evaluations for roughly 814 banks, or about 40 percent of banks now subject to those reviews. Raising the large-bank threshold above $10 billion would reclassify an additional 417 banks, ending their separate investment and service tests and their annual CRA reporting of small-business loans. Only the largest 6 percent of banks would remain subject to separate reviews of community development lending and investment, branch services, and CRA small business loan reporting.
And it could be even worse. Federal regulators use several methods to evaluate banks’ compliance with CRA, including assessments of their qualified lending, services, and community development activity. One of these methods, known as the “strategic plan” approach, replaces standard CRA tests with tailored performance goals developed by the bank with community input.
Strategic plans can make sense when the business model does not fit easily within the standard CRA framework. But they also allow banks to propose their own, potentially weaker standards for compliance. The proposal would encourage banks to use this option and allow them to discuss performance goals with regulators before the public has an opportunity to comment.
That concern is heightened by strategic-plan benchmarks, the OCC proposed in December 2025, which NCRC says show how low banks could set their community development financing goals and still receive passing CRA ratings. In a hypothetical scenario involving 69 banks, NCRC estimated that community development financing could fall by as much as $71 billion a year, a nearly 70 percent reduction, if banks reduced their activity to the proposed benchmarks.
Other proposed changes would further narrow what regulators examine. One would remove deposit products from consideration under the service test, meaning examiners would no longer evaluate whether checking and savings accounts are affordable, accessible, or useful to low- and moderate-income customers. The proposal would also limit retail lending reviews to a bank’s major product lines, offering two alternatives for determining which products would qualify. Under one alternative, examiners would generally evaluate only a bank’s two largest lending categories. That could leave weal performance in mortgage, small-business, or farm lending subject to little scrutiny, even where those loans are critical to a particular community.
The proposal would also reduce the number of banks required to report data on small-business, small-farm, and community development loans. NCRC estimates that this would eliminate 11 percent of CRA small-business lending data nationwide. These data are vital to communities, researchers, and regulators, who use them to evaluate a bank’s lending patterns, identify banking deserts, and detect potential discrimination. Banks also rely on the data for the peer comparisons used in CRA exams and for market research on competitors.
There are also broader proposed changes that would affect banks supervised by the OCC or FDIC, regardless of size. For example, the proposal would eliminate the purpose test, allowing financing for an eligible small business to receive community development credit without showing that it creates, preserves, or improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people, or people in low- and moderate-income areas. Under current guidance, small-business financing generally must meet both a size test and a purpose test to qualify as an economic development activity under CRA.
But Wait: There’s More
These are just a few of the changes the proposal would make. As is common with federal rulemaking, it also includes a section called “Request for Feedback.” Several of its questions ask whether regulators should go even further.
For instance, if you’re worried about the proposal raising the large-bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion, Question 1 asks whether regulators should raise it to $30 billion instead. It also asks whether the small-bank threshold should rise from the proposed $1 billion to $10 billion.
Then—and this one might interest many readers—Question 10 asks whether federal regulators should “eliminate all grants and donations from CRA consideration.”
How to Respond
We know that banks and bank financing are critical to meeting communities’ affordable housing and economic development needs. Banks have the scale, resources, and geographic reach to make a meaningful impact in the communities they serve.
Any CRA rule should require banks to show that they serve their entire communities through fair lending, affordable banking, branches and services, and meaningful investments in affordable housing and community development. Banks should not be able to pass their CRA exams by doing well in one area while neglecting the others.
Advocates can join NCRC in calling on the agencies to halt this rulemaking. Comments can be submitted here. The deadline is Oct. 13.
True to our mission, we have established a campaign website to defend CRA, where you can find a sample comment letter, an interactive map showing the likely impact in your state, a social media tool kit, and information on how to contact federal, state, and local representatives.
As part of the comment process, we are calling on the agencies to extend the current comment period by at least 60 days, giving all interested parties enough time to conduct their own analyses and submit meaningful comments.
Beyond submitting comments, please share your stories of how CRA has made a difference in your community. We know CRA has played a vital role in advancing affordable housing and community building for nearly half a century. We cannot afford to take CRA for granted now.

title: The fish skin that becomes one with your body
content: Guðmundur Fertram Sigurjónsson, an inventor and CEO originally from a small Icelandic fishing village, was looking at fish scales for wound healing, and realised fish skin is structurally similar to human skin. And this makes it an interesting alternative for dressing wounds. Unlike conventional wound dressings – which need to be replaced, potentially damaging fragile new tissue – North Atlantic cod skin stays on the wound. The body's cells grow into it, and as new human tissue develops, the cod skin is gradually absorbed and replaced by the patient's own living tissue. Humans have used animal skin to cover wounds since as far back as the 16th century. Pigs became the dominant donor in modern medicine, largely for their affordability as well as their similarity to human skin. But while mammal skin needs to undergo harsh treatment to eliminate the risk of disease transmission, cod skin may carry little risk of spreading disease to humans, since certain pathogens adapted to cold-water fish struggle to survive in the warmer human body, Sigurjónsson explained to us. What the science says Using fish skin instead of mammal skin may reduce the risk of disease transmission because fish are biologically more distant from humans. However this doesn't necessarily mean fish skin is safer or more effective, Dimitri Beeckman, professor of nursing science at Örebro University and Ghent University, told us. So far, more than 100 scientific studies have looked at fish skin. The largest randomised trial to date, partly funded by Kerecis (a company founded by Sigurjónsson), included 255 patients with deep diabetic foot ulcers. After 16 weeks, 44% of wounds treated with fish skin had healed, compared with 26% with standard care. After 24 weeks, those figures rose to 55% and 38% respectively. Yet more clinical research is needed to establish whether fish skin can really be used as an alternative to products made from pig or human tissue. “There have been some direct comparisons, including with porcine material, but these were mainly small studies using experimental wounds in healthy volunteers,” said Beeckman. From Iceland to the frontlines That doesn't stop Sigurjónsson from applying the method in practice. He founded his company Kerecis in 2013, and has since worked with humanitarian organisations, hospitals, and surgeons. Today, Kerecis has an expanding presence in Europe and across the world. According to Sigurjónsson, Kerecis has treated hundreds of thousands of patients worldwide using fish skin. They've donated their fish skin product to Ukrainian patients who have suffered injuries and are being treated in Ukraine and in neighbouring countries. Because fish skin is lightweight, has a long shelf life, and can be stored at room temperature, it is particularly useful for treating wounds in war zones. The price of healing faster So why is fish skin as wound treatment not more widespread? Cost is one important factor, as it is generally more expensive than standard care, although this depends on the healthcare system. “Costs and reimbursement differ between countries, and more independent health-economic research would be useful,” Beeckman told us. Fish-skin grafts are a promising addition to standard care for selected patients, according to Beeckman. But more independent trials, real-world evidence, and research into cost and benefits are needed.

title: What's making it harder for American family farms to survive
content: By — Judy Woodruff Judy Woodruff By — Sarah Clune Hartman Sarah Clune Hartman Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/whats-making-it-harder-for-american-family-farms-to-survive Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Transcript Audio For generations, the family farm has been central to the American story. But these days, farmers are struggling with sharply higher costs and crushing debt on top of the same economic pressures the rest of the country feels. Judy Woodruff reports on what it takes to keep a farm going and who will carry on the tradition. It's part of her series, Crossroads: America at 250. Read the Full Transcript Notice: Transcripts are machine and human generated and lightly edited for accuracy. They may contain errors. Amna Nawaz: For generations, the family farm has been central to the American story. But, these days, farmers are struggling with sharply higher costs and crushing debt, on top of the same economic pressures the rest of the country feels.Judy Woodruff reports from Western Kansas on what it takes to keep a farm going and who will carry on the tradition. It's part of her series Crossroads: America at 250. Cole Carpenter, Triple C Farms: This corn should be six feet tall. Judy Woodruff: There's no corn harvest for Cole Carpenter this fall after a severe drought this summer stunted its growth. Cole Carpenter: It's tough, no matter which way you look at it. Judy Woodruff: For generations of Americans, farming was a way of life, work the land, make a living, and pass it on. At the nation's founding, nine in 10 Americans were farmers. Today, fewer than 2 percent are.Sarah Mock, Author, "Farm (and Other F Words): The Rise and Fall of the Small Family Farm": To Thomas Jefferson, America was always an agricultural experiment. We were always going to be the agricultural powerhouse of the world, and that was going to be the bedrock of our nation. Judy Woodruff: We met agricultural journalist Sarah Mock at Old Town Farm in Albuquerque, New Mexico, a former horse farm turned into a cafe and event space. Sarah Mock: Jefferson crafted this, like, yeoman idea of people who are close to the land and therefore have this, like, sense of community and loyalty and patriotism that had really not been seen by Europeans in like hundreds of years. Cole Carpenter: Yes, farming is a gamble. Judy Woodruff: I first met Cole Carpenter at his farm near Leoti, Kansas, 20 years ago, when I was reporting for a documentary about millennials. Cole's grandfather, Dale Appl, had been farming for decades. The land had been in his family since the late 1800s. But even in 2006, there were doubts about whether farming could support the next generation. Dale Appl, Farmer: And I told him he ought to have another profession. He could still farm on the side. And he might have to yet. I don't know. It's pretty tough. Judy Woodruff: Twenty years later, the Carpenters are still farming. They have expanded it 10,000 acres, added cattle, and a crop spraying business. But margins are slim. Two years ago, Cole and his wife, Bridget, sold 800 acres to put capital back into the operation.Was that a tough decision? Cole Carpenter: Oh, yes, 100 percent, yes, yes. I mean, that -- it doesn't go easily. But at the same time, the less debt, the less stress was an easier decision there. Judy Woodruff: Around them, larger operations bought up smaller farms, mirroring a national trend. The number of farms in the U.S. declined 10 percent between 2012 and 2022 to about 1.9 million. At the same time, the average size grew by 5 percent. Cole Carpenter: And it felt like we were on an island. Like, land is being gobbled. Judy Woodruff: All around you. Cole Carpenter: Around you. One of my grandpa's biggest thing was, he always said, don't worry about what the neighbors are doing or what's going on around you. Take care of what you have, keep working, and you will be fine. Judy Woodruff: Now just 4 percent of farms, the largest family operations, account for more than half of all agricultural sales. And Carpenter says the challenge isn't just producing more. It's paying for everything it takes to do it. Cole Carpenter: All the technology, all the seed we have, we're able to grow more, but it also comes with a cost. Judy Woodruff: But even with all the latest technology, those who work the land still face risks they can't control. Cole Carpenter: You can stick your hand in. Judy Woodruff: Weather, commodity prices, land costs, politics, and tariffs. Cole Carpenter: At the end of the day, we don't really have any control over what the price of wheat is today or the price of corn is. I think the American farmer and rancher is kind of caught in a wicked loophole. You know what I mean? We're just trying to survive. Sarah Mock: Jefferson's idea of how farms were going to work lasted well into the late 1800s. We really thought it's going to be fine, there's always going to be land, anyone who wants it and who has the right effort and the grit is going to have their chance. Judy Woodruff: That idea at our founding depended on one thing: There was always more land to take. But by the late 1800s, that was changing.Still, that classic image of the farmer has endured, independent, self-sufficient, and deeply rooted to the land, as seen in Grant Wood's iconic American Gothic, a painting of a stoic farmer and his daughter in 1930. Narrator: In the Wheat Belt, farmers face ruin. Judy Woodruff: But the reality has always been more complicated. The Dust Bowl and the Great Depression devastated farming, forcing many farmers off their land. The federal government stepped in and fundamentally reshaped farming into a larger, more mechanized industry. Sarah Mock: And that is basically the road we have been on since then. Farms have continued to get bigger. We have seen a huge drop-off in the total number of farmers. Judy Woodruff: And if you don't inherit land, Mock says, it is nearly impossible to make it. It's a story she explores in her book "Farm (and Other F Words): The Rise and Fall of the Small Family Farm." Sarah Mock: So I started out doing research for this book thinking, what can I learn about conventional agriculture and teach to first-generation farmers? What's the secret sauce? How do you make a farm last?And not spoil it, but it's money. Tim Peterson, Cedar Crest Farms: This is a used one. Judy Woodruff: It's a reality 71-year-old farmer Tim Peterson of Monument, Kansas, knows all too well. Tim Peterson: We have this mythical sense of what farmers are and what they do, and I think there's just -- people don't quite understand how financially and business-orientated it is nowadays. It's -- I don't know if you need quite an MBA to run a farm, but it's getting close. Judy Woodruff: He and his wife, Rebecca are facing the once unthinkable, the possibility of selling family land to pay down about $800,000 of debt. Tim Peterson: It's really hard, actually, because you give up opportunities. You give up an opportunity into the future. You will not be able to ever buy that land back. Some of the land we would sell, oh, my, well, it's been in the family certainly since the 1920s, so over 100 years, easy. Judy Woodruff: For his daughter Lydia, who works in Topeka, this land is part of her family's legacy.Lydia Peterson, Daughter of Tim Peterson: I think it's inspiring to think about all of the blood, sweat and tears my great grandparents have put into the land, and then my grandparents, several generations of hard work that the land represents. Judy Woodruff: Last fall, Lydia tried to buy back a piece of family land at an auction, but instead of the expected $350,000 price tag, it sold for $540,000. Tim says the economics of farming have become increasingly unpredictable. Tim Peterson: We will be up maybe $130,000 and then we're down $60,000 the next. Judy Woodruff: It's that volatile? Tim Peterson: Yes, it's quite volatile, and because of the crop prices and the yield. We're all -- we're really dependent on yields. Judy Woodruff: The costs of staying in business can be enormous. Nationwide, farm debt has risen sharply, up an estimated 70 percent from 10 years ago. Tim Peterson: What really kind of scares me in terms of American farming is the fact that -- the consolidation of the industry. That troubles me a lot. If you have got a farm that has 120,000 acres versus a farm that has 1,800 acres, all of a sudden you lose that diversity and the decision-making. Cole Carpenter: I mean, this obviously has withstood. Judy Woodruff: And yet the next generation hasn't given up. Cole Carpenter's sons, Huck, age 15 and Chase, 18, are still in high school, but say they want a farm. They would be the sixth generation to work on this land. Huck Carpenter: The big corporations around us are always trying to expand and take over more territory. So keeping our ground and being financially stable, it's going to be difficult. Chase Carpenter: From my grandpa to my great-grandpa, it's always been how proud this family farm was, and how we have always rolled through punches and just always came out on the end. Judy Woodruff: But their dad, just like his grandpa 20 years ago, wants them to have a choice. Cole Carpenter: I want them to be happy in whatever they do, whatever way they want to go. I hope it's coming back here. But at the same time, if it's not, that's fine, because I think life's too short to be trying to do something that you don't want to do to make somebody else happy. Judy Woodruff: And for Sarah Mock, there's something even deeper at stake, the connection that comes from knowing a particular piece of land. Sarah Mock: Being close to land and not just owning it by having the deed, but owning a place by knowing it, by being able to say, like, oh, I know where that turn in the river is. Nothing makes you more patriotic than knowing the land. Judy Woodruff: For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Judy Woodruff in Leoti, Kansas. title: ‘Tem que taxar os bilionários’: Marcha pelo Clima leva debate sobre mudanças climáticas e eleições às ruas de Brasília
content:
Sob um pé de mangueira e com temperatura de 29ºC, ativistas, movimentos sociais, servidores públicos e candidaturas distritais e federais participaram neste domingo (20) da Marcha pelo Clima, realizada no Eixão do Lazer, na altura da 102 Sul, em Brasília (DF). O encontro começou às 10h e terminou por volta das 13h, após os manifestantes percorrerem o Eixão por cerca de 15 minutos e interromperem a marcha por conta do calor.
Durante o ato, os participantes entoaram o coro: “Tem que taxar os bilionários; É culpa deles que tá quente pra caralho”.
A manifestação abordou mudanças climáticas, modelo econômico e eleições. Os participantes também defenderam a inclusão da pauta ambiental no debate eleitoral.
Ian Coelho, do Jovens pelo Clima, uma das organizações que mobilizaram a marcha, relacionou o ato ao debate eleitoral. “É muito bonito ver essa mobilização nesse dia quente que vai ficar mais quente com El Niño”, afirmou.
Segundo ele, o movimento fez um chamado “contra o capitalismo” e pela inclusão da pauta climática nas eleições. “É um chamado pra mobilização, pra lutar contra os pecuaristas, lutar por um novo mundo que é possível”, disse.
Lúcia Mendes, do Fórum de Defesa das Águas, do Clima e Meio Ambiente do Distrito Federal, organização que liderou a mobilização pela proteção da Serrinha do Paranoá, afirmou que o planeta vive “o limiar da maior crise climática que esse planeta já viu”.
A área da Serrinha do Paranoá foi incluída pelo Governo do Distrito Federal (GDF) entre imóveis públicos cogitados para capitalizar o Banco de Brasília (BRB) e cobrir prejuízos associados a negociações com o Banco Master.
Ela também comparou a crise climática a uma nova pandemia. “O mundo está assistindo as eleições no Brasil com atenção, nós já vimos o que custou de vidas colocar um aventureiro bandido na presidência do Brasil. Agora mais uma pandemia, a pandemia climática”, declarou.
Ao falar sobre o modelo econômico, afirmou: “Não dá mais para ser refém do sistema capitalista, que só pensa em acúmulo de riqueza”.
A Marcha pelo Clima foi realizada em 16 cidades brasileiras durante o final de semana. A mobilização reuniu organizações, movimentos populares e trabalhadores em defesa da justiça climática, meio ambiente, da vida e dos povos, e também como uma forma de chamar a atenção para a importância do tema no debate eleitoral.
A Campanha Vote Pelo Cerrado, representada pelas organizações Rede Cerrado, Instituto Sociedade População e Natureza (ISPN), Funatura e Campanha Nacional em Defesa do Cerrado, esteve presente cobrando o compromisso de candidatos e candidatas do DF para a defesa do bioma.
“Cobramos o compromisso com pautas muito específicas, que vão desde a questão hídrica, passando pelo desmatamento até a garantia de direitos”, explicou Ingrid Silveira, secretária executiva da Rede Cerrado.
Política ambiental e eleições
Joana Tanure, servidora do Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima (MMA), relatou mudanças ocorridas na estrutura do ministério durante a gestão de Jair Bolsonaro.
“A gestão passada extinguiu a secretaria do clima do MMA no segundo dia, colocou todos os servidores numa sala sem computador, sem trabalho, deixou de lado um monte de servidores que atuavam na questão climática”, afirmou.
Joana classificou a situação como “perseguição institucional” e disse que foi “muito difícil atuar com a questão climática no governo passado”.
Bruno Ferreira Farias, candidato aprovado no concurso do Instituto Chico Mendes de Conservação da Biodiversidade (ICMBio) de 2024 e representante da comissão de aprovados que reivindica a convocação dos novos servidores, falou sobre a composição do Congresso Nacional. “Além do Lula, é necessário que se eleja um congresso de esquerda também. Executivo e legislativo fundamental”, afirmou.
Claudia Trindade, profissional com 33 anos de carreira e especialista em meio ambiente, com passagem pelo ICMBio e pelo Ibama e integrante da Associação Nacional dos Servidores da Carreira de Especialista em Meio Ambiente (Ascema) e da Asibama-DF, falou sobre a falta de servidores na área ambiental. “Temos pouquíssimos servidores para unidades de conservação. Todos os governos têm uma grande dificuldade de fazer concurso para esse trabalho”, afirmou.
Matheus Adugo, da Associação Indígena Areme Eda, do povo Bororo, que vive no Setor Noroeste de Brasília, defendeu a retomada da cosmovisão dos antepassados indígenas.
“A gente precisa trazer de volta a cosmovisão dos nossos antepassados, que não pensavam só no agora”, afirmou.
Adugo também falou sobre a participação política nas eleições. “Uma das ferramentas, e não é a única solução, é o voto consciente. É votar pelo clima”, disse. “Se a gente não pensar no clima, não será possível pautar outras coisas”, afirmou.
Segundo ele, a falta de atenção à questão climática pode levar a consequências ambientais futuras. “Daqui a um tempo vai sobrar poeira, cinza, queimada, fumaça”, declarou.
Maktus Fabiano, militante do Juntos e diretor do Diretório Central dos Estudantes (DCE) da Universidade de Brasília (UnB), também relacionou as eleições à pauta climática.
“É fundamental que, nesse momento das eleições, a gente não deixe de lado a questão climática”, afirmou.
Maktus reforçou que o fenômeno climático do “super El Niño” deixa mais evidentes os efeitos das mudanças climáticas. Ele defendeu a superação do sistema capitalista e afirmou que, em sua avaliação, o sistema é responsável pelas mudanças climáticas e pela violência contra povos indígenas e quilombolas.
“Apenas uma revolução ecossocialista está à altura dos desafios que temos que enfrentar”, declarou.
“Nessa etapa do capitalismo, do império capitalista que tá em crise, nossa aposta é mobilização das ruas”, afirmou.
Maktus comparou o capitalismo a “uma locomotiva rumando ao fim do planeta” e disse que a organização popular é necessária para “puxar o freio de mão”.
Mila Monteiro, ativista da Sociedade Vegetariana Brasileira (SVB), falou sobre a relação entre pecuária e desmatamento.
“A pecuária é a maior responsável pelo desmatamento”, afirmou, lembrando que a maior parte “de tudo que é plantado nesse país é pra alimentar gado”.
“Se a gente quer floresta de pé, é preciso tirar animal do prato”, disse.
Durante a marcha, também houve uma intervenção de apoiadores de candidaturas de direita. No início do ato, um bloco de apoiadores de Flávio Bolsonaro passou pelo local da concentração. Houve troca de provocações entre os grupos. Na ocasião, manifestantes entoaram: “Flávio ladrão, seu pai tá na prisão”.
Candidatos a deputado federal, distritais e organizações da sociedade civil como Instituto Arayara, Movimento de Atingidos por Barragens (MAB), Diretório Central Acadêmico da UnDF, bloco de Maracatu do Boiadeiro Boi Brilhante, também participaram da atividade.

title: Learning to Move Cities: Deep Meta-Models and Reinforcement Policies for Calibration and Control in Urban Networks
content: Urban transportation networks present complex optimization challenges spanning calibration of high-fidelity simulators and real-time operational control. This paper presents a shared latent-space framework that connects simulator calibration and reinforcement learning control through a common learned representation of urban traffic dynamics. First, we develop a combinatorial MLP-autoencoder architecture that learns low-dimensional manifolds linking simulator inputs (origin-destination demand, network parameters) to outputs (travel times, congestion patterns), enabling efficient Bayesian optimization for calibration. This approach demonstrates superior sample efficiency compared to traditional dimension reduction methods, achieving better fit to observational data within fixed computational budgets. Second, we implement a deep Q-learning agent with experience replay and target networks to optimize dynamic traffic assignment through scheduling and routing adjustments. In empirical evaluations on benchmark networks, our approach reduces system-wide travel times by up to 51% compared to baseline operations. The learned latent representation is not only used to reduce the dimensionality of Bayesian calibration, but is also incorporated into the reinforcement learning state representation, allowing the control policy to operate on compressed and calibrated traffic dynamics. This shared latent-space formulation provides a unified pathway from simulator calibration to adaptive operational control within intelligent transportation systems. Our results highlight the transformative potential of deep learning methods in urban mobility planning and management, particularly for large-scale networks where traditional optimization approaches face computational bottlenecks.

title: GeneSIS: enhancing transferability of polygenic scores with variant-level gene-by-sex interaction effects
content: Advancing precision medicine requires accurate prediction of disease liability across populations and contexts. A major challenge is the limited transferability of polygenic scores (PGS) across genetic ancestry groups. We present GeneSIS (GENE and Sex Interaction Score), a supervised statistical learning framework for jointly modeling additive and context-dependent genetic effects at single-variant resolution directly from individual-level data. We analyze 406,659 individuals, including admixed individuals, in the UK Biobank and 1.3 million variants to develop predictive models for 99 complex traits. We report that ~8% of selected variables capture gene-by-sex (GxS) effects, validated by sex-stratified analyses. Modeling GxS effects improves prediction across 32 traits in non-European individuals. For predicting hip circumference in Africans, GeneSIS achieves a 3.7-fold improvement (p=8.0x10-7) over linear-only PGS and highlights biologically plausible hypotheses, such as pleiotropic GxS effects of GCKR (rs1260326) on anthropometry and menopause, as well as GxS pathway enrichments for interleukin-4 regulation. Overall, our results highlight the benefits of integrating context-dependent effects in human genetics studies.

The assistance was provided by partners from Austria, Azerbaijan, Belgium, the United Kingdom, Denmark, Estonia, Ireland, Iceland, Spain, Italy, Canada, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, North Macedonia, Poland, Slovakia, Türkiye, Finland, France, Czechia, Switzerland and Sweden.

As reported, between June and August, critical infrastructure facilities in various regions received equipment worth a total of €74.79 million through the Energy Support Fund.

title: Guyana strengthening global partnerships to fight cancer – Dr Anthony
content:
Health Minister Dr Frank Anthony has said that the Government of Guyana is strengthening partnerships with leading global health institutions as part of its ongoing efforts to improve cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment in the country.
He made the remarks on Wednesday, during the launch of Pinktober, an annual, month-long observance held every October to raise awareness about cancers across the country.
“We have a very strong partnership with Mount Sinai; we’re benefitting from their experience. We have another partnership with Northwell, and these are two global institutions that have been first-class in how they manage patients with cancer, and more recently we also developed a partnership with MD Anderson, and they came down, and they were working with the team so that we can perfect what we’re doing in terms of cervical cancer. They’ve helped us to reorganise and so forth. So, we’re working with some of the best institutions in the world to help us to beat cancer here in Guyana,” the health minister said.
He highlighted that the Government also has a strong partnership with McMaster University.
“They have been going back and forth with us; they come down, they bring teams, and they work with us,” he noted.
He added that the Government has developed a “good partnership” with the National Cancer Institute of India.
“They sent down a team, and we’re going to expand a lot of the work that we’re doing with them. They’re willing to train local people; they’re gonna bring people from India to work with the local team, expand training for persons, whether nurses, doctors, and they’re also gonna take people from here to India to train at their institutions. So, that partnership is ongoing. And there are patients who would have various complications; they’ve been taking some of our patients too and managing them in India,” he outlined.
Most recently, Dr Anthony said the Government has partnered with France through the European Union.
“We now have a partnership with Agency France, and they have a project with us called HealthNext, and with HealthNext we have been bringing a lot French expertise to Guyana, and our intention is to send some people out to France to be trained, and among the institutions that have been working with us is the Marie Curie Institute, as you know, that’s one of the top institutes dealing with cancer, and they’re now one of the partners we’ve been working with. Just recently, about two weeks ago, we had a doctor from Toulouse that came in and was working with our team to look at cancers in gynaecology, and so they would be structuring a programme and coming back and doing a lot of training and teaching and so forth,” the health minister explained.
For the year so far, 704 persons have been diagnosed with various forms of cancer. Prostate, breast, cervical and colorectal represent a combined 46 per cent of those diagnoses.
Anthony emphasised that the Government is working to improve citizens’ access to screening, strengthen diagnostic services, and expand available treatment options.
“We’re don’t just know that you have a problem and not do anything about it. We’ve been taking a lot of proactive measures, and we continue to expand what we are doing, and we’re working with different partners to create different options,” he noted.

title: La tecnología geoespacial impulsa el nuevo circuito de F1 de Madrid y la gestión urbana de Fuenlabrada
content:
La plataforma ArcGIS de Esri ha permitido a las empresas ACCIONA y Eiffage construir el circuito de Fórmula 1 MADRING con alta precisión, mientras que el Ayuntamiento de Fuenlabrada la ha implantado junto a la inteligencia artificial para gestionar su movilidad urbana y la Zona de Bajas Emisiones.
Ambos casos de éxito se presentarán en la Conferencia Esri España 2026 los días 30 de septiembre y 1 de octubre en IFEMA (Madrid).
Índice de temas
Precisión y gemelos digitales en el circuito MADRING
Para afrontar la construcción del circuito de F1 de Madrid en un entorno urbano de alta complejidad y bajo estrictos criterios ambientales, ACCIONA y Eiffage utilizaron ArcGIS de Esri como plataforma centralizada.
El proyecto combinó el uso de drones para procesar imágenes con fotogrametría y modelos 3D para supervisar los movimientos de tierra. Además, la plataforma permitió elaborar un inventario geoespacial del arbolado afectado e integrar modelos BIM y GIS para crear un gemelo digital vivo que detectó interferencias durante las obras.
Inteligencia artificial y visión unificada en Fuenlabrada
Por su parte, el Ayuntamiento de Fuenlabrada ha adoptado la tecnología GIS como sistema operativo para la gestión de la ciudad, integrando inteligencia artificial geoespacial a través de la iniciativa Fuenlabrada Lab.
La solución incluye un gemelo digital vivo que centraliza y combina datos del sistema de control de la Zona de Bajas Emisiones (ZBE) con indicadores de tráfico, transporte público y ruido. Esto permite disponer de una visión unificada del municipio, comprender mejor los patrones de movilidad y mejorar la transparencia hacia la ciudadanía.

title: In Savannah, Georgia’s utility regulators faced public wrath over data centers
content:
Georgia’s Public Service Commission, or PSC — the group that has final say over how the state’s largest electric utility generates electricity and how much it charges customers — regularly hears from members of the public during its meetings. But because those meetings are almost always in Atlanta, many of the commenters typically come from the metro area.
Since the spring, commissioner Alicia Johnson, one of two recently-elected Democrats, has been pressing the commission to meet in a different part of the state as a way to open the floor to different commenters. On Tuesday, the PSC finally did that.
“For over 100 years, the Public Service Commission has met in Atlanta and rarely, if at all, has meetings across the state,” Johnson, whose PSC district includes Chatham and Effingham counties, said. “This was an opportunity for me to have our commissioners come out and actually speak with their constituents outside of Atlanta to move away just from hearing the voices of interveners or advocates.”
The commissioners traveled to Savannah to hear from coastal residents. Following a brief administrative meeting and a presentation on the PSC’s recent actions on data centers, including approval of Georgia Power’s contract with OpenAI and new protections for regular customers, the floor opened for public comments.
Many of those who spoke voiced concerns over the OpenAI data center that is planned for Effingham County, just outside of Savannah, and called for more transparency around the company’s contract with Georgia Power — the largest for a single customer since the utility started reporting its contracts in 2024.
“There’s a reason you’re named the Public Service Commission and not the Georgia Power service commission or the OpenAI service commission,” said Bill Wright of Pooler, a city northwest of Savannah. “Your name tells you where your loyalty should lie.”
The commissioners clarified the limited scope of their involvement with data centers: They oversee the making and selling of electricity only if a data center chooses Georgia Power as its utility. They encouraged attendees to take up their concerns with local elected officials.
Commenters also criticized the commission over power bills.
Michael Hawthorne, an organizing strategist with the Sierra Club, argued the commission is supposed to set reasonable rates for electricity. Then he posed a question to the room at large.
“Does anybody feel like everything’s reasonably priced?” he asked.
The audience replied with a resounding “No.”
The frustration and anger from the Savannah crowd wasn’t surprising, Johnson said.
“It’s what I’ve heard since running for office, and so I’m just glad that our other commissioners got to hear some of it, too,” she said.
Jason Shaw, a Republican from a south Georgia district and the PSC chair, said the meeting reinforced what he’s heard from constituents as well. In an interview after the meeting, Shaw said transparency has been a core issue with the OpenAI data center in particular, starting at the local level. But he said Georgia Power needs to share more information about its data center contracts, too.
“We’ve got to do a better job of forcing the company to be able to present more to us that’s not redacted,” he said. “And I think that’s something that we’re working really closely on.”
Some commenters accused the commissioners of failing to represent the interests of the public that elected them — and reminded them another election is coming up in November.
“If you truly want to be on this board, it’s time to step up and protect the people,” said Corey Foreman, a candidate running for the state senate from a coastal district. “If you can’t do that, I will be more than happy to help remove you.”
All five members of the PSC were Republicans from 2006 until the start of this year, when Peter Hubbard and Johnson took office after unseating two Republican incumbents in an election that focused largely on power bills and the commission’s recent history of rate increases. The two Democrats have cast dissenting votes several times and closely questioned Georgia Power officials. But both have also been candid that their ability to shift policy on emissions, rates, data centers, and other issues is limited while they are in the minority on the PSC.
The District 3 seat currently held by Hubbard and the District 5 seat recently vacated by Republican Tricia Pridemore are both on the ballot in November. If the Democratic candidates win both seats, the party would hold a majority on the commission for the first time in decades.
Hubbard was elected to a one-year term last year and is now facing former Republican commissioner Fitz Johnson in a rematch election for a six-year term. In District 5, Democrat Shelia Edwards is running against Republican Josh Tolbert. While the candidates have to live in their districts, both races are statewide.
Early voting begins October 13.

title: Referendum gegen neue AKWs kommt laut Bündnis zustande
content:
Damit dürfte die Stimmbevölkerung an der Urne über die AKW-Frage befinden können.
Der «Tagesanzeiger» berichtete zuerst über den Sammelstand. Das Bündnis «Nein zu neuen AKW» bestätigte diesen am Samstag in einem Communiqué. Die AKW-Gegnerschaft hätte noch fast drei Wochen Zeit gehabt, um die für ein Referendum nötigen 50'000 Unterschriften zu sammeln.
Hinter dem Referendum stehen die SP, die Grünen, die GLP, Teile der Mitte-Partei sowie zahlreiche Organisationen wie die Schweizerische Energie-Stiftung und Greenpeace Schweiz. Sie bekämpfen den vom Parlament denkbar knapp verabschiedeten Gegenvorschlag zur Volksinitiative «Jederzeit Strom für alle (Blackout stoppen)».
Dieses Begehren haben die Initianten inzwischen bedingt zurückgezogen. Der Gegenvorschlag erfülle das Kernanliegen der Initiative - die Aufhebung des Kernkraftwerk-Verbots - bereits, hiess es.
Das Bündnis «Nein zu neuen AKW» wiederum wirft dem Bundesrat und dem Parlament vor, am Willen der Bevölkerung vorbei zu politisieren. Die Stimmberechtigten hätten sich im Rahmen von vergangenen Abstimmungen klar für eine auf erneuerbaren Energien basierende Zukunft ausgesprochen, hiess es in ihrer Mitteilung.
Die Beteiligten planen, die Unterschriften am 6. Oktober bei der Bundeskanzlei einzureichen. Kommt das Referendum offiziell zustande, dürften die Schweizer Stimmberechtigten frühestens am 28. Februar 2027 über die Gesetzesänderung abstimmen können.

title: Rare century-old Mildura housing scheme directs lease revenue to local schools
content:
Rare century-old Mildura housing scheme directs lease revenue to local schools
In short:
Mildura is the only Australian town where a college lease scheme remains.
There are 184 blocks of land in the north-west Victorian city that are leased to raise funds for local schools.
What's next?
Some housing experts say the scheme could be introduced elsewhere to improve housing affordability.
In Victoria's tropical north, where the Murray River winds, a select group of houses are selling for half of what you'd expect.
It's got nothing to do with changes in the housing market and can trip up even the most savvy investor.
The unusual house prices are thanks to the 140-year-old legacy of two Canadian engineers who decided education should be the benefactor of their entrepreneurial endeavours.
Mildura's college lease scheme is unique.
No other Australian town has one.
In the citrus capital, 184 lots are leased to individuals and organisations instead of being sold freehold.
Basically, someone can own the improvements but not the land itself.
Officially, the land is owned by the Victorian education minister.
Revenue from the lease agreements goes directly to schools in Sunraysia, which use the funds to buy new classroom equipment and technology that they would otherwise go without.
A Department of Education spokesperson said the Mildura Schools Land Trust disburses about $1.95 million annually to 27 primary and secondary schools, providing additional funding that benefits more than 9,000 students.
A lofty deal
In 1886, the Victorian government signed a deal with Canadian engineers George and William Chaffey to build the Mildura irrigation settlement.
Historian and former primary school principal Bob Walton said the Chaffey brothers set aside one-fifteenth of available land to generate funds for an agricultural college, although this was never built.
Instead, a local high school became the first to benefit from the lease funds.
"They decided to set aside and not sell some of the allotments in the colony," he said.
"The Chaffeys were very interested in education."
Mr Walton said the Chaffey brothers were inspired by a similar scheme in California, their base before coming to Australia.
'Cheap' prices grab buyer attention
College lease properties often appear in real estate listings for what, at first glance, seem like a bargain price.
One home recently sold for a reported $300,000 on Mildura's Lemon Avenue where, across the road, a similar freehold property fetched almost $550,000 two months earlier.
"Obviously, there's lease land for other things, but not like this. This is very unique," Ray White Mildura managing director Damian Portaro said.
"It's interesting having to explain to a buyer from Melbourne or Sydney exactly what this is.
"It's 100 years old now, this system. It was probably ahead of its time back then, but I haven't seen it or heard of it anywhere else."
Mr Portaro said the property listings appealed to first home buyers, but they often ran into difficulty obtaining finance due to the unusual lease clause.
He said most buyers of college lease land were investors rather than owner-occupiers.
"They might get in for half the price, for example, then they start factoring in 'there's rates, there's insurances, there's a college lease I have to pay.'"
Unlocking housing supply
Mallee Accommodation and Support Program (MASP) has utilised the scheme to build social housing on five college-lease properties with assistance from Homes Victoria.
"We see it as a really good way to have two social goods out of the one block of land — both continuing to support local schools and also building social and affordable housing onto it," chief executive Charmaine Calis said.
MASP told a parliamentary inquiry last year the Victorian government should look at more ways college leases could ease the housing crisis.
"We do need to increase the supply of housing available, and this is certainly one way we can look at doing that," Ms Calis said.

title: 11,297 acres returned to Maine’s Penobscot Nation after more than a century
content:
A vast stretch of Maine forest has changed hands in a return more than a century in the making. On September 16, 2026, 11,297 acres surrounding the East Branch of the Penobscot River were returned to the Penobscot Nation, marking the first phase of a larger effort to restore more than 30,000 acres of ancestral homeland. The Trust for Public Land, which is partnering with the Penobscot Nation on the project, said the wider effort began in 2023 with a $32.5 million fundraising goal. So far, $20.7 million has been raised, with additional funding still needed to complete the remaining phases.
A first step toward returning more than 30,000 acres
The 11,297-acre transfer is part of the Wáhsehtəkʷ land-return effort, named for the East Branch of the Penobscot River. The property lies near the base of Katahdin and just south of Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument. The first phase covers an area roughly comparable in size to the city of Portland, Maine. It includes about 15 miles of cold-water streams, 865 acres of ponds and wetlands, and habitat used by species including Atlantic salmon, brook trout and moose.
The project is being carried out through a partnership between the Penobscot Nation and the Trust for Public Land. The conservation organisation purchased the broader property from timber harvesters after it came onto the market more than three years ago, while working with the Nation to raise the money needed to return the land.
The partnership's broader goal is to return more than 30,000 acres to the Penobscot Nation. Completing that effort will require another $12 million, according to the Trust for Public Land and Maine Public.
Land with cultural and environmental importance
The returned property is significant not only because of its size but also because of its connection to Penobscot culture and the East Branch of the Penobscot River. The Nation plans to take an active role in caring for the landscape, including restoring habitats around waterways and monitoring wildlife and ecological conditions. Planned work includes tracking ticks and monitoring bat populations, alongside broader efforts to protect habitats and waterways.
The land also creates opportunities for Penobscot citizens to access natural resources. Those plans include hunting, harvesting and potential economic development, according to Chuck Loring, the Penobscot Nation's natural resources director, as reported by Maine Public. For the Nation, the difference between advising on conservation and actually owning the land is significant. Ownership gives the Penobscot Nation greater authority over how the property is managed and conserved.
The 11,297-acre transfer is part of the Wáhsehtəkʷ land-return effort, named for the East Branch of the Penobscot River (Image Credit: Chris Bennett/ Trust for Public Land)
A potential new route to Katahdin Woods and Waters
The land return could also affect access to the nearby Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument. One long-term possibility is the creation of a southern access route through the returned land near Millinocket. Currently, there is no southern access route into the monument, and the proposed connection could eventually make the area easier to reach.
However, the access-road proposal is still in development. Details regarding its route, construction and timing have not yet been finalised. According to the Trust for Public Land, improved access could also benefit communities around the Katahdin region by making it easier for visitors to reach the monument and potentially increasing activity for local businesses, including restaurants, lodging providers and outdoor recreation operators.
Part of a larger Wabanaki land-return effort
The Penobscot project is also connected to a broader effort involving Maine's Wabanaki Nations. The Wáhsehtəkʷ project forms part of Tributary Land Returns, a collaboration involving the four federally recognised Wabanaki tribes in Maine and seven conservation organisations. The wider initiative seeks to return more than 50,000 acres through 11 projects.
The Penobscot Nation currently stewards approximately 140,000 acres, according to the Trust for Public Land. The organisation said the four Wabanaki Nations collectively hold only about 1% of their ancestral lands in Maine, placing the current project within a much larger history of land ownership and restoration. The partnership also reflects a shift in how conservation organisations approach Indigenous communities. Rather than treating tribes only as advisers or stakeholders in conservation projects, land-return initiatives place ownership and stewardship directly in tribal hands.
What happens next
The September 2026 transfer completes only the first phase of the Wáhsehtəkʷ project. The partners are continuing to raise money for the remaining land, with the overall campaign targeting $32.5 million and $20.7 million already secured. Once the full project is completed, more than 30,000 acres around the East Branch of the Penobscot River could be under Penobscot ownership and stewardship.
For the Nation, the returned 11,297 acres represent more than a large tract of Maine forest. The property reconnects Penobscot people with land, waterways and natural resources tied to their culture, while creating opportunities for conservation, recreation and future economic activity. The first transfer therefore marks both the completion of one phase and the beginning of the next: a continuing effort to return the remaining acreage and restore Penobscot ownership across a much larger part of the ancestral landscape.

title: [Magazine] En Indonésie, des photos d’animaux contre de l’argent
content:
Dans la forêt tropicale de Bornéo, un programme de conservation de la faune incite des villageois à photographier ou enregistrer les animaux qui vivent là. En contrepartie, ces petits agriculteurs touchent une rémunération qui les «aide vraiment».
Octavius s’enfonce dans la forêt de Bornéo, un téléobjectif fixé à son téléphone pour photographier orangs-outans, oiseaux et félins, une mission pour laquelle il reçoit de l’argent dans le cadre d’un programme de conservation de la faune. Le projet KehatiKu consiste à rémunérer des particuliers dans neuf villages du district de Kapuas Hulu, dans la province de Kalimantan occidental, pour des photos ou des enregistrements d’animaux. Les paiements vont de 5 000 roupies (environ 0,24 euro) pour l’observation d’un oiseau commun à 130 000 roupies (6,37 euros) pour un orang-outan menacé d’extinction, la récompense maximale.
Les observateurs les plus actifs peuvent gagner jusqu’à 10 millions de roupies (490 euros) par mois, soit plusieurs fois le revenu moyen d’un ouvrier agricole. La plupart des participants, comme Octavius, âgé de 50 ans, sont de petits agriculteurs cultivant du riz, du cacao, du durian et du kratom, une plante aux effets stimulants. Ce supplément de revenus «aide vraiment, surtout pour payer les études universitaires de mes enfants», confie Octavius.
Le programme, géré par le cabinet de conseil en environnement Borneo Futures, a débuté il y a deux ans et produit des données sur la répartition de la faune et l’évolution des populations animales. Il vise également à faire des agriculteurs et des chasseurs des acteurs de la conservation, au sein de communautés qui capturent depuis longtemps des oiseaux chanteurs pour les vendre. «Les gens commencent à comprendre qu’auparavant, ils capturaient un oiseau qui valait 50 000 roupies, alors qu’aujourd’hui, il leur suffit de prendre une photo et de nous l’envoyer pour recevoir un paiement de 5 000 à 10 000 roupies par oiseau», explique Nardiyono, directeur de Borneo Futures Indonesia. «S’ils prennent seulement cinq photos, ils gagnent 50 000 roupies et l’oiseau reste dans son environnement, demeure observable et conserve sa capacité à se reproduire», indique-t-il encore, soulignant que les revenus potentiels tirés de l’observation des oiseaux «sont donc bien supérieurs à ceux issus de leur chasse».
Le programme est financé par des fondations philanthropiques et a reçu environ 300 000 dollars (260 000 euros) à ce jour, précise Borneo Futures. La moitié de cet argent a été consacrée au développement, notamment de l’application permettant de télécharger les signalements et d’un système d’IA aidant les humains à vérifier les observations. Jusqu’à maintenant, plus de 350 000 observations ont été transmises, dont environ la moitié a été validée et rémunérée.
J’ai mes propres revenus… je ne dépends donc pas de mon mari
En septembre, Octavius et des dizaines d’autres habitants avaient rendez-vous devant le minuscule bureau municipal de Labian, qui compte 683 habitants, pour recevoir leurs paiements mensuels. Pour cette fois, il a touché quatre millions de roupies, soit un peu moins de 200 euros. «C’est une activité secondaire, cela n’interfère pas» avec les travaux agricoles, indique-t-il, en montrant une parcelle où il cultive du kratom et du cacao. «Parfois, lorsque nous travaillons, nous entendons des oiseaux chanter, alors nous nous approchons pour les observer. Si nous pouvons prendre une photo, nous le faisons. Sinon, nous nous contentons d’un enregistrement sonore», également rémunéré.
Le modèle du programme est «probablement plus favorable, tant sur le plan environnemental que social, qu’une conception de projet de conservation sans mesures incitatives», explique Paul Ferraro, chercheur à l’université américaine Johns-Hopkins de Baltimore. Le principal défi sera de maintenir le financement, ajoute-t-il. «Les gens pourraient revenir à leurs anciens schémas comportementaux, car les mesures incitatives financières sont insuffisantes une fois que l’enthousiasme est retombé», met en garde cet expert en comportement humain et en politiques publiques.
Pour l’instant, Borneo Futures dispose d’un financement garanti jusqu’en 2028 et deux villages supplémentaires rejoindront le programme en octobre. L’initiative finance l’observation de 73 espèces, notamment des oiseaux, des singes, des félins sauvages et des cervidés.
Antonia Uneng explique qu’elle n’a jamais besoin de s’éloigner beaucoup de sa maison de Sungai Ajung, un village de moins de 400 habitants entouré de terres agricoles et de forêt tropicale, pour effectuer ses observations qui l’ont aidée à acheter son premier réfrigérateur. Cette femme de 36 ans s’est également offert une machine à karaoké, loisir très populaire en Indonésie et qui occupe une place de choix dans son salon. Le projet a ainsi donné aux femmes du village un sentiment d’indépendance, ajoute Antonia, dont le mari travaille à l’étranger. «J’ai mes propres revenus… je ne dépends donc pas de mon mari», se réjouit-elle.

title: Valdés: "El futuro forestal que tiene Corrientes va a marcar un nuevo rumbo en la industrialización"
content:
El gobernador de Corrientes, Juan Pablo Valdés, encabezó el acto central y desfile cívico militar por el centenario de la imposición del nombre a la localidad de Gobernador Ingeniero Valentín Virasoro. El mandatario puso en relieve el desarrollo industrial de la provincia.
Tras suspender la cláusula gatillo docente, Zdero busca prohibirla por ley en Chaco
La ceremonia, desarrollada frente a la plaza Libertad junto al intendente local Guillermo De la Cruz, contó con la presencia de autoridades provinciales, delegaciones escolares, fuerzas de seguridad y vecinos que conmemoraron el primer siglo de historia de la comuna.
En el marco de los festejos, la Provincia de Corrientes y el municipio formalizaron la firma de un convenio para la construcción de 20 nuevas soluciones habitacionales. Durante su alocución, el mandatario ponderó el desarrollo industrial de la zona y remarcó la importancia de dejar de ser simples proveedores de materia prima para avanzar en el agregado de valor en origen.
Desarrollo forestal, nuevas tecnologías y obras de infraestructura
Al evaluar el crecimiento de las actividades productivas de la zona norte, el titular del Ejecutivo destacó el liderazgo de la industria yerbatera y el potencial del sector maderero. "Estoy convencido de que el futuro forestal que tiene la provincia, y especialmente Virasoro, va a marcar un nuevo rumbo en la industrialización de la madera y un nuevo rumbo en la oportunidad para nuestras familias", afirmó Juan Pablo Valdés, al tiempo que valoró la llegada al puerto de Corrientes de tecnología para la primera planta industrial de madera contralaminada (CLT) del país.
Jorge Asís: “Pagano se hastió para encarar la epopeya higiénica de la aniquilación”
Asimismo, el gobernador anunció la ejecución del proyecto para el bypass o avenida circunvalación de la ciudad. La obra vial es considerada prioritaria para desviar la circulación del transporte de carga fuera de la planta urbana y acompañar el movimiento logístico de la producción.
Inversión pública y compromiso de la comunidad
Respecto del rol del Estado provincial frente al avance del sector privado, el mandatario ratificó la decisión de sostener las inversiones en servicios e infraestructura comunitaria. "Necesitamos que, cuando esas oportunidades lleguen, encuentren a los correntinos y a los virasoreños preparados", enfatizó al convocar a los sectores productivos a consolidar el polo industrial.
Duro cruce entre Oría y Cachanosky: "Resentido" y "¿conocés la palabra dignidad?"
Por su parte, el intendente Guillermo De la Cruz remarcó la importancia de las familias pioneras que cimentaron la economía de la región y convocó a la ciudadanía a asumir un rol protagónico en la proyección de la localidad. Tras los discursos oficiales, la jornada continuó con el tradicional paso de las instituciones y el desfile de las fuerzas armadas sobre la avenida principal.

title: Angélica María y Angélica Vale visitan la Parroquia de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria en Guatemala
